title: Wild Swimming in Pembrokeshire
strapline: Dive into crystal-clear waters and hidden coves: Pembrokeshire's wild swimming scene awaits.
metaTitle: Wild Swimming Pembrokeshire | Secluded Coves | Adventure Wales
metaDescription: Discover the best wild swimming pembrokeshire has to offer! From the Blue Lagoon to Barafundle Bay, find secret spots and essential tips.
heroAlt: A wild swimmer emerges from the turquoise waters of the Blue Lagoon, Pembrokeshire, with slate cliffs in the background.
introduction:
Pembrokeshire Coast National Park isn't just about clifftop walks; it's a wild swimming paradise. The rugged coastline, dotted with secluded coves and boasting unbelievably clear water (on a good day!), makes it ideal for both seasoned wild swimmers and adventurous beginners. What sets Pembrokeshire apart is the sheer variety: you can hurl yourself into the exhilarating depths of the Blue Lagoon, paddle gently in the sheltered waters of Barafundle Bay, or explore hidden sea caves at low tide. 

However, it's not all sunshine and lollipops. Pembrokeshire waters can be surprisingly cold, even in summer, and the Atlantic swells can turn a millpond into a washing machine in a heartbeat. Respecting the sea is paramount. If you're new to wild swimming, stick to sheltered spots and consider a guided tour with one of the local outdoor activity centres. 

Wild swimming Pembrokeshire is best suited to those who enjoy a bit of adventure. You might have to scramble down rocks, navigate slippery seaweed, and keep an eye on the tides. It's perfect for independent spirits who appreciate the raw beauty of the Welsh coastline and the invigorating feeling of immersing themselves in nature. Be warned – the post-swim pasty from The Shed is dangerously addictive. Finding parking near some of the more popular spots can be a nightmare in the summer, so arrive early or be prepared to walk. And don’t even think about swimming after a heavy rainfall, the water quality plummets.

Embrace the wild, respect the sea, and prepare for an unforgettable wild swimming pembrokeshire experience. You might even spot a grey seal! Don't forget that final piece of wild swimming Pembrokeshire advice - always check the tides!
topTips: Wear a wetsuit even in summer. Sea temperatures here peak around 15-16°C in August and sit at 10-12°C over winter, so a lot of first-timers underestimate the cold shock, especially at exposed spots like Whitesands and Aber Mawr.

The Blue Lagoon looks tame from the car park but it isn't. It's a flooded slate quarry roughly 25m deep with submerged rock and debris, and uncontrolled jumping ('tombstoning') sends several people to hospital most years, with Coastguard helicopter and RNLI callouts a regular occurrence. If you jump, only do it from the marked, lower platforms, enter feet-first like a pencil, and never jump if you haven't checked the water below first.

Download the Safer Seas & Rivers Service app (Surfers Against Sewage) and check it before any swim. It gives real-time sewage discharge alerts for Pembrokeshire's bathing waters — never swim within 48 hours of a heavy-rain discharge alert or after prolonged heavy rainfall, when run-off tanks water quality across the coast.

Parking is the single biggest headache in peak season. Abereiddy, Whitesands and Barafundle's Stackpole Quay car park all fill by mid-morning in July and August — arrive before 10am or you'll be turned away or queuing on narrow lanes.

Tides genuinely change these beaches. Marloes Sands and Barafundle both lose most of their sand at high water, and at Marloes the sea can cut off sections of beach — always check tide times before you commit to a full day, not just before you get in the water.

Beginners should stick to sheltered, low-current spots: Barafundle Bay, Caerfai Bay and Porthgain harbour are the forgiving options. Save Whitesands, Aber Mawr, Marloes Sands and Druidston Haven for when you're confident reading swell and currents.

Wear old trainers or neoprene boots, not bare feet. Weever fish bury themselves in sandy shallows and give a nasty sting if trodden on, and several of these beaches (Porthgain, the Blue Lagoon, Stackpole) have rocky or slipway entries that will shred bare soles.

Bring cash or a card for pay-and-display — Whitesands, Porthgain and Marloes Sands car parks all charge, and several of the smaller free car parks (Aber Mawr) fill within an hour of a sunny forecast breaking, so have a plan B spot in mind.

firstTimer: Start at Barafundle Bay or Caerfai Bay. Both have sheltered, relatively calm water and an easy, obvious entry, which makes them far less intimidating than swimming off open, swell-exposed beaches like Whitesands.

Always swim parallel to the shore, not straight out, and use a brightly coloured tow float so boats and other swimmers can see you — none of these spots have permanent lifeguard cover outside the main summer season.
A wetsuit isn't optional gear here, it's the difference between a 20-minute swim and a 5-minute one. Even in August the water is cold enough to trigger cold water shock if you go in without one.

Check the Met Office Coastal Forecast and a surf/swell report before you leave, not just the general weather app on your phone — Pembrokeshire's exposed west-facing beaches (Whitesands, Aber Mawr, Druidston) can look fine on a general forecast and still have dangerous swell.
Tell someone on land where you're swimming and roughly how long you'll be, especially at quieter spots like Aber Mawr or Druidston Haven where there's no one else around if something goes wrong.

Budget extra time for parking and the walk in. Barafundle is a half-mile walk from the Stackpole Quay car park, and Druidston involves a steep path down the cliff — factor that into when you set off, not just your swim time.

If in doubt, join a guided session with TYF Adventure or Preseli Venture in St Davids. It's the easiest way to learn safe entry and exit points, tide reading and cold-water technique from people who swim here year-round.
Pack warm layers, a hat and a hot drink for after — the shivering ('afterdrop') can hit 10-15 minutes after you get out, once your core temperature keeps dropping even out of the water.
regular: Skip the Blue Lagoon crowds by walking round the headland south of Abereiddy car park — there are quieter rock platforms and gullies with the same turquoise water and none of the queue for the jump spot.
Swim Whitesands or Marloes Sands early morning before the surf schools and day-trippers arrive — by 10am in summer both beaches are a different, busier place.

After heavy rain, Porthgain harbour is often your best bet — it's sheltered by the old harbour walls and doesn't churn up the way open beaches do, though check the Safer Seas app first as harbours can hold run-off too.

Druidston Haven and Aber Mawr are the two spots locals treat as their quiet alternatives to Barafundle and Whitesands — same quality of water, a fraction of the people, at the cost of a longer walk in.
Combine Stackpole Quay with the coast path walk to Barafundle Bay and on to Broad Haven South for a proper half-day out — swim at both ends and you avoid doubling back to the same car park.
Autumn swims (September-October) often have the calmest, clearest water of the year once the summer crowds thin out — sea temperature is still holding from summer but the car parks are empty.

For a longer or more technical swim, check conditions with TYF Adventure or Preseli Venture before heading to Aber Mawr or Marloes Sands — both spots can flip from calm to genuinely dangerous swell within a tide cycle.
If you're chasing seals, Marloes Sands and the waters off Stackpole are your best bet — keep well back and never approach a seal on the rocks, they'll abandon a haul-out spot if repeatedly disturbed.

spots.name: Blue Lagoon (Abereiddy)
spots.description: The flooded slate quarry offers an unforgettable swimming experience. Jump from the varying cliff heights (carefully!), explore the deep, turquoise waters, and feel the rush of the waves. It's incredibly popular so expect company, but the setting is truly unique.
spots.bestFor: Thrill-seekers, experienced swimmers looking for a unique setting, those who enjoy a crowd.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners in rough weather, those with a fear of heights, anyone who hates crowds.
spots.parking: Abereiddy beach car park. Can get VERY busy. £5 for the day, arrive before 10am in peak season or park further away and walk.
spots.insiderTip: Walk around the headland to the south for some quieter swimming spots and a different perspective on the lagoon. Be careful on the rocks!
spots.howToDoIt: From the car park, follow the short path down to the old quarry workings and pick a spot along the rock ledges to get in — there's no beach, so most people enter from rock or one of the low platforms. Swim a lap of the lagoon to take in the slate cliffs, or head to the seaward end where a gap in the rock connects to the open sea (only attempt this on a calm day and be aware of surge). If you want to jump, only use the marked lower platforms, check the water for submerged rock first, and jump feet-first with arms crossed — higher, unofficial jump points are where the serious injuries happen.
spots.access: Free public access via Abereiddy Beach car park, a short walk from the water's edge. No lifeguard cover. The quarry is deep (around 25m in places) with submerged rock and old quarry debris near the edges, so check depth before jumping and never dive head-first into unfamiliar water.
spots.routeDescription: A roughly oval flooded quarry around 100m long, ringed by slate cliffs 3-12m high. Deepest water is toward the centre and the seaward end; shallower, rockier margins run around the sides where most swimmers get in and out.

spots.name: Barafundle Bay
spots.description: Often voted one of the UK's best beaches, Barafundle boasts golden sands and crystal-clear, sheltered waters. It's a bit of a walk to get there, which keeps the crowds at bay. Perfect for a relaxing swim and sunbathing.
spots.bestFor: Families, beginners, those seeking a beautiful and relatively safe swimming spot.
spots.notSuitableFor: Those with mobility issues (due to the walk), surfers looking for waves.
spots.parking: Stackpole Quay National Trust car park. £5 for non-members. About a half-mile walk to the beach.
spots.insiderTip: Pack a picnic and stay for the day. The sunset over Barafundle is magical.
spots.howToDoIt: Park at Stackpole Quay and follow the half-mile coast path over the headland down to Barafundle's sands — there's no vehicle access to the beach itself. The bay is sheltered by headlands on both sides, so entry is straightforward off the sand; swim close to shore and parallel to the beach for the calmest water, or head toward the rocks at either end for a bit more interest at high tide.
spots.access: No direct road or car access to the beach — it's reached only via the coast path from Stackpole Quay (National Trust car park, charge for non-members) or from Broad Haven South to the south. At high tide the sand narrows considerably, so check tide times if you want beach space as well as swimming.
spots.routeDescription: Half-mile coast path walk from Stackpole Quay, gently undulating with a short climb over the headland, before dropping down through dunes and pine trees to the beach. The swim itself is a sheltered, curving bay roughly 300m across.

spots.name: Aber Mawr
spots.description: A secluded, north-facing beach known for its dramatic scenery and good surf. The swimming can be good here, but only when the waves aren't too big. It's often quieter than other beaches in the area.
spots.bestFor: Experienced swimmers, surfers (when there are waves), those seeking solitude.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families with young children in rough weather.
spots.parking: Small car park near the beach. Free, but fills up quickly. Limited space to park along the road.
spots.insiderTip: Check the surf report before you go. This beach can get some serious waves.
spots.howToDoIt: Park at the small car park and follow the short path down through the dunes to the beach. Check the surf and swell forecast before you set off — on a calm day this is a lovely, quiet swim close to shore; with any groundswell running it turns into a proper surf beach with a shorebreak and rip potential, so assess conditions from the sand before getting in.
spots.access: Small free car park a short walk from the beach; it fills quickly on good-weather days and there's limited overflow parking along the approach road. North-facing and exposed to Atlantic swell, so conditions here change more with the forecast than at sheltered south-coast spots.
spots.routeDescription: A wide, curving, north-facing beach backed by dunes and low cliffs either side. Best swimming is in the middle of the bay away from the rockier margins at each end, which hold more current when there's any swell.

spots.name: Caerfai Bay
spots.description: A small, sheltered bay with colourful cliffs and relatively calm waters. It's a popular spot for families and a good place to learn to swim. The purple sandstone cliffs are striking.
spots.bestFor: Families, beginners, those seeking a safe and scenic swimming spot.
spots.parking: Caerfai Farm campsite car park. Small charge. Limited parking along the road.
spots.insiderTip: Head to the nearby St Non's Chapel and Well for a bit of history after your swim.
spots.howToDoIt: Park at Caerfai Farm campsite and take the short path down to the small sand-and-shingle beach. The bay is sheltered by the surrounding cliffs, so entry is easy off the sand and it's a good spot to practise sighting and short swims close to shore before venturing to more exposed beaches.
spots.access: Reached via Caerfai Farm campsite car park (small charge) with limited additional roadside parking. The bay is naturally sheltered, making it one of the calmer swimming spots on the St Davids peninsula even when other beaches are getting wind and swell.
spots.routeDescription: A compact bay beneath layered purple-red sandstone cliffs, with a sand and shingle beach that narrows at high tide. Swimming is mostly close-in and sheltered, with the open sea beyond the bay mouth for stronger swimmers.

spots.name: Whitesands Bay
spots.description: A large, sandy beach with powerful waves, popular with surfers. The swimming is best on calmer days, but be aware of strong currents. Lifeguards patrol in the summer.
spots.bestFor: Experienced swimmers, surfers, those who enjoy a lively beach atmosphere.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families with young children on rough days.
spots.parking: Whitesands Bay car park. Can get very busy. Pay and display.
spots.insiderTip: Check the lifeguard flags before you enter the water. Respect the currents.
spots.howToDoIt: In peak season, swim between the red and yellow flags where RNLI lifeguards patrol — this is by far the safest way to swim here given the beach's exposure and currents. Outside the flagged, patrolled hours (and outside the summer season), treat Whitesands with real caution: check the surf forecast, watch for rip currents forming near the rocks at each end of the bay, and don't swim alone.
spots.access: Large pay-and-display car park directly behind the beach. Lifeguard cover typically runs the main summer season only (check current dates before relying on it) — outside those times you're on your own for safety, so conditions and experience matter more.
spots.routeDescription: A long, open, west-facing sandy beach around 1km across, backed by dunes with Carn Llidi rising behind. Currents and rip potential are highest near the rocky points at the north and south ends; the safest, flattest water is usually mid-beach.

spots.name: Porthgain harbour
spots.description: Swim within the historic harbour walls for a unique experience. The water is usually calm and sheltered, offering a safe and interesting swim with views of the old brickworks.
spots.bestFor: Beginners, families, those seeking a sheltered and historical swim
spots.notSuitableFor: Those looking for a natural beach experience, strong wave lovers
spots.parking: Porthgain car park. Can be busy, but turnover is decent. Pay and display.
spots.insiderTip: After your swim, reward yourself with fish and chips at The Shed – it's legendary.
spots.howToDoIt: Enter from the slipway or steps inside the harbour walls — this is one of the easiest, most sheltered entries on this list, which makes it a good spot to acclimatise to open water without dealing with waves or a long walk-in. Stay inside the harbour for a short, calm swim, or, if conditions and experience allow, head out past the harbour mouth into open water — only do this on a calm day and be aware of boat traffic in the channel.
spots.access: Pay-and-display car park right by the harbour, level walk to the water. The harbour walls give year-round shelter from swell, though water quality can dip after heavy rain like anywhere on this coast, so check the Safer Seas & Rivers app first.
spots.routeDescription: A small, walled harbour with calm water inside and open sea just beyond the entrance. Swimming inside the walls is a short, flat loop; venturing past the harbour mouth adds exposure to swell and boat traffic.

spots.name: Stackpole Quay
spots.description: Swim around the picturesque Stackpole Quay. The water is clear and relatively calm, perfect for a short dip. You can explore the little harbour and enjoy the views of the surrounding coastline. Note that this is also the access point for Barafundle.
spots.bestFor: Beginners, families, those seeking a quick and scenic swim
spots.notSuitableFor: Those looking for a long swim or challenging conditions
spots.parking: Stackpole Quay National Trust car park. £5 for non-members.
spots.insiderTip: Combine your swim with a walk to Barafundle Bay or Broad Haven South for a longer adventure.
spots.howToDoIt: Enter via the slipway by the quay for a short, sheltered dip around the harbour, or use it as a warm-up before the coast path walk to Barafundle Bay. It's shallow and calm close to the quay, making it a good spot for a quick, low-commitment swim rather than a long session.
spots.access: National Trust car park right at the quay (charge for non-members), level access to the water via the slipway. Very sheltered compared to open beaches nearby, so a reliable fallback if wind or swell rules out Barafundle or Whitesands.
spots.routeDescription: A small stone quay and harbour with calm, clear water. Swim a short loop around the harbour, or head out a little further toward open water on a calm day for better views of the coastline.

spots.name: Marloes Sands
spots.description: A vast, sandy beach with dramatic rock formations. The swimming can be good, but be aware of strong currents and the open sea. Explore the rock pools at low tide.
spots.bestFor: Experienced swimmers, those who enjoy exploring rock pools, wildlife enthusiasts.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families with young children on rough days.
spots.parking: Marloes Sands National Trust car park. Pay and display.

startPoint.name: Marloes Sands National Trust Car Park

spots.insiderTip: Keep an eye out for seals! They're often spotted in the area. Check the tide times before you go to make the most of the beach and rock pools.
spots.howToDoIt: Walk down from the National Trust car park to the sands and choose your entry point depending on the tide — at low tide there's a huge expanse of beach and rock pools to explore before you even get in the water. Swim close to the main beach area away from the rockier headlands, and treat any currents around the rock outcrops with caution as this is an open, west-facing beach.
spots.access: National Trust pay-and-display car park with a walk down to the beach. The beach is tidal — at high water the sand largely disappears and the sea reaches the base of the cliffs in places, so plan your visit around tide times rather than just arrival time.
spots.routeDescription: A large, west-facing sandy beach with dramatic layered rock formations and sea stacks. Best swimming is mid-beach; the rockier ends and outcrops hold more current and are better explored on foot at low tide than swum around.

spots.name: Druidston Haven
spots.description: A beautiful, secluded beach backed by towering cliffs. The swimming can be good, but be aware of the tides and the potential for strong waves. It's a bit of a walk down to the beach, which keeps it relatively quiet.
spots.bestFor: Experienced swimmers, those seeking solitude, surfers (sometimes).
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families with young children on rough days, those with mobility issues (due to the walk).
spots.parking: Druidston Hotel car park (small charge) or limited parking along the road.
spots.insiderTip: Stay at the Druidston Hotel for a clifftop retreat with stunning views. The restaurant is excellent.
spots.howToDoIt: Follow the path down from the hotel car park or roadside parking to the beach below — it's a steeper, longer approach than most spots on this list, which is exactly why it stays quiet. Check swell and tide before you go: this is an open, exposed beach, and conditions can shift from calm to genuinely rough within a tide cycle, so don't assume a good forecast in St Davids means the same conditions here.
spots.access: Access is via a path down from the Druidston Hotel car park (small charge) or limited roadside parking above — no direct vehicle access to the beach. The walk down (and back up) is the main practical barrier, which is why it's one of the quieter spots even in peak season.
spots.routeDescription: A long, open beach beneath high, dramatic cliffs, reached by a fairly steep clifftop path. Swimming is best attempted mid-tide when there's enough sand to enter easily but before the sea narrows against the cliff base at full high water.

practicalInfo.weather: Pembrokeshire weather can be unpredictable. The sea temperature is cold year-round, usually peaking around 15-16°C in August. Strong winds and swells can make swimming dangerous, so always check the forecast and sea conditions before you go. Coastal fog is also common, so be prepared for reduced visibility.
gearChecklist: Wetsuit (essential for most of the year)
Neoprene gloves and socks (for extra warmth)
Towel (a quick-dry microfibre towel is ideal)
Warm clothes for after your swim (including a hat and gloves)
Brightly coloured swim buoy or tow float (for visibility)
Appropriate footwear (for rocky beaches and coastal paths)
First-aid kit (including antiseptic wipes and plasters)

gettingThere.publicTransport: Haverfordwest and Pembroke Dock are the main train stations. From there, you can catch local buses or the Pembrokeshire Coast Bus (Puffin Shuttle) to reach various coastal locations. The Celtic Coaster bus service is great for exploring the St Davids peninsula.
gettingThere.parkingTips: Parking can be a nightmare during peak season. Arrive early, be prepared to walk, and consider using park-and-ride services where available. Some beaches have National Trust car parks, which are free for members.

practicalInfo.safety: Always swim with a buddy if possible. Be aware of tides, currents, and weather conditions. Check water quality reports, especially after heavy rainfall. Let someone know where you're going and when you expect to be back. In an emergency, dial 999 and ask for the Coastguard. The RNLI provides lifeguard services on some beaches during the summer months. Carry a mobile phone in a waterproof pouch.

faqs.question: What's the average sea temperature in Pembrokeshire?
faqs.answer: The average sea temperature in Pembrokeshire ranges from 10-12°C in winter to 15-17°C in summer. A wetsuit is highly recommended, even in the summer months.

faqs.question: Are there any dangerous marine animals in Pembrokeshire waters?
faqs.answer: While rare, jellyfish are sometimes present. Portuguese Man o' War can occasionally wash up on beaches, but they are easily identifiable. Weever fish can sting if stepped on, so wear shoes or sandals on sandy beaches. Grey seals are common, keep a safe distance and never approach them.

faqs.question: Is it safe to swim in the Blue Lagoon?
faqs.answer: Swimming in the Blue Lagoon is generally safe, but be aware of the depth and potential hazards such as submerged rocks and debris. Check for strong currents, especially after heavy rain. Supervise children closely. Jumping from the cliffs is risky and should be done with caution.

faqs.question: Where can I find the best wild swimming spots for beginners?
faqs.answer: Barafundle Bay, Caerfai Bay, and Porthgain harbour are good options for beginners due to their sheltered waters and relatively calm conditions. Always check the weather forecast and tide times before you go.

faqs.question: Do I need a license or permit to wild swim in Pembrokeshire?
faqs.answer: No, you don't need a license or permit to wild swim in Pembrokeshire. However, be respectful of the environment and follow the Countryside Code. Avoid swimming in areas that are designated as nature reserves or protected areas.

faqs.question: Are there any guided wild swimming tours in Pembrokeshire?
faqs.answer: Yes, several local outdoor activity centres in Pembrokeshire offer guided wild swimming tours. These tours are a great option for beginners or those who want to explore the coastline with an experienced guide.

faqs.question: What should I do if I get into trouble while wild swimming?
faqs.answer: If you get into trouble while wild swimming, try to stay calm and signal for help. If you're with a buddy, work together to reach safety. If you're alone, try to float on your back and conserve energy. If you can, call for help on your mobile phone (if you have signal). If you see someone else in trouble, dial 999 and ask for the Coastguard.

faqs.question: Can I wild swim in Pembrokeshire with my dog?
faqs.answer: Many beaches in Pembrokeshire are dog-friendly, but some have restrictions during the summer months. Check the local signage before you let your dog off the lead. Be aware of strong currents and tides, and make sure your dog is a strong swimmer.
